Education in Entrepreneurship: Necessary or Antiquated?

Everyone and their mother seems to be “working on a startup” these days. Maybe there’s something appealing about the idea of being your own boss, working your own hours, and not having to answer to “The Man.” Some may call it escaping the system, others may call it running to another. Regardless of your views on this renewed entrepreneurial spirit that perhaps subsists a little bit too much on dropshipping and course-selling and not enough on educational attainment followed by its application, it is undeniably shaping the future in ways that are yet unmeasurable. With high-school-aged influencers on social media flaunting stacks of cash and fancy sports cars, the narrative being pushed on us seems to be that education does not equal success (at least when you can sell your fitness course online for $15 a customer). So the question follows: for those of us with that… hustler instinct, what is the right next step? If these adolescents can make more money in a month than the average American does in a year without ever seeing the frontside of a degree (other than the one hanging in their high school principal’s office), it makes you wonder where all that tuition money went. Is education no longer a necessary feature for entrepreneurial success? Or is it time to assuage these anti-education sentiments? The answer, it seems, is that it depends.

The figure below depicts data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor, which interviews over 100,000 entrepreneurs across the globe yearly.

We can see from the depiction the average education level of entrepreneurs per country measured against the average perceived ease of starting a business. The entrepreneurs in countries that appear higher on the graph on average believe it easier to start a business, and the entrepreneurs in countries to the right are generally more educated. At first glance, there seems to be no apparent relationship between education and ease of starting a business. We can actually confirm this by calculating the correlation between education and perceived ease of starting a business, which comes out to 0.012. This correlation indicates an essentially negligent relationship between education and perceived ease. It would seem from this that the more educated an individual is does not necessarily translate to how easy it would seem to them to start a business.

If we take a look, though, at the countries highlighted in red, we can see an interesting result. According to Pitchbook data, these countries are home to the top 100 entrepreneur-producing schools globally. Yet, there still seems to be no visible correlation. It seems that when we control for education, we still can’t account for the varied ease of starting a business. Education seems to help in some cases, and it doesn’t seem to help in others. Some people may be convinced at this point. Education has no effect on the behavior of entrepreneurs. After all, don’t they always say it’s who you know, not what you know? Let’s look at the graph below and see if that’s really true.

This graph depicts the average network of entrepreneurs across the globe, on a scale of “none” to “few” to “many”. Bars highlighted green are in the 50th percentile or above in terms of entrepreneurial ease. We still see green staggered throughout the entire depiction, indicating that it is not in fact who you know. The larger ones network does not indicate ease of starting a business.

In addition, returning to the Pitchbook Top 100, we can see that the countries (in red) that produce the most successful entrepreneurs do not show any correlation at all between network and success.

In the charts above, I want to highlight in particular the countries of Israel (IL), South Africa (ZA), and South Korea (KR). Israel, one of the most highly educated countries, also seems to be one of the ones in which it is hardest to start a business. And yet, as seen in the table below, it has eight schools on the Pitchbook Top 100 list. South Africa and South Korea, two of the most poorly connected countries according to the GEM dataset, also both contain schools in the Pitchbook Top 100.
